core: Behaviorism's founding commitment: learning studied as observable behavior in relation to environmental events
Classical (respondent) conditioning: Pavlov's conditioned reflexes; Watson's extension to human emotion
Operant conditioning: Thorndike's law of effect; Skinner's operant behavior and the antecedent-behavior-consequence contingency
The four operant contingencies and the correct reading of 'positive' and 'negative' as added and removed
Classroom applications: behavior-specific praise, token systems, PBIS, and IDEA's requirement to consider PBIS
Honest limits: behaviorism brackets internal processes, evidence quality for specific practices varies, and the extrinsic-reward debate is unresolved
supporting: Functional definition of reinforcers and punishers (defined by effect on behavior, not by adult intent)
Applied behavior analysis and behavior support planning as places operant principles still live
Extinction as inhibition rather than erasure (spontaneous recovery, renewal)
outOfScope: Social learning theory and Bandura's modeling research (separate topic in this unit)
Therapeutic, clinical, or diagnostic advice, including individualized guidance about behavior intervention for a specific child
Learning-styles claims, which the subject source-map flags as unsupported

claims.claim: Behaviorism, as Watson set it out in 1913, proposes that psychology should be an objective natural science of observable behavior aimed at prediction and control, and that it should not depend on introspection or on consciousness as its subject matter.

Pavlov received the 1904 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for work on the physiology of digestion; his observation of 'psychic secretion' led him to the study of conditioned reflexes, which he continued until his death in 1936.

In classical conditioning a neutral stimulus paired with a psychologically significant event comes to elicit a response on its own; the response is elicited rather than emitted, so the learner does not have to act for the pairing to take effect.

Thorndike's law of effect states that a behavior followed by a satisfying effect becomes more likely to be repeated; operant (instrumental) conditioning associates a behavior, rather than a stimulus, with a consequence.

In operant conditioning, reinforcement increases the future probability of a behavior and punishment decreases it, while 'positive' means a stimulus is added and 'negative' means a stimulus is removed - the terms describe the operation, not whether the outcome is pleasant.
Operant behavior comes under stimulus control: a discriminative stimulus sets the occasion for a response without eliciting it in the way a conditioned stimulus does.
Shaping reinforces successive approximations toward a target behavior; secondary reinforcers such as tokens acquire their value through association and are the basis of token-economy systems.

Among partial reinforcement schedules, variable-ratio schedules produce the highest response rates and the greatest resistance to extinction, while fixed-interval schedules produce the lowest response rates.

Extinction weakens a conditioned response but does not erase the original learning: spontaneous recovery and the renewal effect show the response can return after time passes or when the context changes.

Reinforcer devaluation studies show that learners encode the specific outcome a behavior produces rather than simply having responses automatically stamped in, which contradicts the strongest version of the early behaviorist account.

Under IDEA, when a child's behavior impedes that child's learning or the learning of others, the IEP team must consider the use of positive behavioral interventions and supports and other strategies to address that behavior.

PBIS is a tiered framework supported by a technical assistance center funded by the U.S. Department of Education, in which Tier 1 practices include teaching and acknowledging expected behavior schoolwide, Tier 2 provides targeted support, and Tier 3 provides intensive individualized support.

A 2023 brief from the Center on PBIS concludes that Tier 1 PBIS can be designated an evidence-based practice for reducing exclusionary discipline and improving social, emotional, and behavioral outcomes; the brief was produced by the center that supports the framework.

The 2008 IES What Works Clearinghouse practice guide on reducing behavior problems in elementary classrooms rates 'modify the classroom learning environment' and 'teach and reinforce new skills to increase appropriate behavior' as supported by strong evidence, and rates identifying triggers, collaborating with colleagues and families, and schoolwide strategies as moderate.

A 2019 systematic review of 30 studies (11 methodologically sound by CEC and WWC standards) found insufficient evidence to classify teacher praise as an evidence-based practice for K-12 students without severe disabilities, and no discernible pattern for when or for whom praise is effective.

A 1999 meta-analysis of 128 experiments found that engagement-contingent, completion-contingent, and performance-contingent rewards undermined free-choice intrinsic motivation (d = -0.40, -0.36, -0.28), that positive feedback enhanced free-choice behavior (d = 0.33) and self-reported interest (d = 0.31), and that tangible rewards tended to be more detrimental for children than for college students.

Researchers on the other side of the reward debate argue that detrimental effects of reward occur only under restricted and avoidable conditions and that conditioning mechanisms account for both increases and decreases in task motivation.

A 2014 meta-analysis (k = 183, N = 212,468) reported that intrinsic motivation predicted performance whether or not incentives were present, that intrinsic motivation mattered less when incentives were directly tied to performance and more when they were indirectly tied, that incentives better predicted quantity while intrinsic motivation better predicted quality, and that incentives and intrinsic motivation are not necessarily antagonistic.

The Watson and Rayner 'Little Albert' study is historically famous but its identification and interpretation have been disputed in later historical scholarship, so it should not be taught as a clean demonstration.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether extrinsic rewards undermine intrinsic motivation
positions: Deci, Koestner, and Ryan (1999): across 128 experiments, expected tangible rewards significantly reduced free-choice intrinsic motivation, with children more affected than college students; positive verbal feedback increased it.
Eisenberger and Cameron (1996): detrimental effects appear only under restricted, easily avoidable conditions, and conditioning mechanisms explain both the increases and the decreases.

Cerasoli, Nicklin, and Ford (2014): intrinsic motivation predicted performance regardless of incentives, with crowding out when incentives were directly tied to performance; incentives and intrinsic motivation are best considered together rather than as opposites.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as an open disagreement. The lesson reports the effect sizes and the competing interpretations, and teaches the design question (how the reward is contingent, and on what) rather than declaring a winner.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How strong the classroom evidence for praise actually is
positions: The 2008 IES practice guide rates teaching and reinforcing replacement behaviors as supported by strong evidence.
Moore et al. (2019) found insufficient methodologically sound evidence to call teacher praise on its own an evidence-based practice for K-12 students without severe disabilities.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both are reported. The lesson distinguishes a broad recommendation about teaching and reinforcing skills from the narrower question of whether praise alone meets formal evidence-based-practice criteria, and notes that insufficient evidence is not evidence of harm.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether early behaviorism's account of learning is mechanistically complete
positions: Classical behaviorism treats consequences as strengthening responses without appeal to internal representations.
Reinforcer-devaluation research shows learners encode the specific outcome a response produces, implying expectancy-like learning.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson labels behaviorism as a historical school whose principles remain useful in application, while stating plainly that the strong 'stamping in' account is not supported by later evidence.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Status of the Watson and Rayner 'Little Albert' study
positions: Traditional textbook treatment as a demonstration of conditioned fear in an infant.
Later historical scholarship disputes the identification of the child and the interpretation of the results.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Mentioned briefly as historically important and contested, with a note that it could not be conducted under current research ethics.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's framing of behaviorism as a generic 'concept students use to organize information' - no source treats behaviorism this way, and the draft contained no actual theory content.
The draft's vocabulary entries ('context', 'evidence', 'application') were generic study-skills terms rather than behaviorist terminology.
The draft's quick-check items tested only the generic idea of 'defining a term and applying it', not any behaviorist principle.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the boilerplate draft with the actual theory: classical vs operant conditioning, the four contingencies, schedules, shaping, and extinction.
Added an explicit, repeated correction of the most common error in this topic - reading 'negative' as 'bad' rather than as 'a stimulus is removed'.
Added the functional definition of reinforcement and punishment, so that consequences are classified by their effect on behavior rather than by the adult's intent.
Labeled behaviorism as a historical school while identifying where operant principles remain in current U.S. practice and law (WWC guidance, PBIS, IDEA).
Added a limits section that reports the reward debate with real effect sizes on both sides and does not resolve it.

sourceRecords.title: Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It (1913)
sourceRecords.provider: John B. Watson, Psychological Review; reproduced by Classics in the History of Psychology (York University)
sourceRecords.notes: Primary 1913 statement of the behaviorist program: psychology as an objective natural science of behavior, aimed at prediction and control, that sets aside introspection and consciousness. Used for the claim that behaviorism brackets internal mental processes by design. Article text is from 1913 and is in the public domain in the United States; no prose was reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Ivan Pavlov - Biographical, The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1904
sourceRecords.notes: Confirms Pavlov's 1904 prize was awarded for work on the physiology of digestion, that his study of 'psychic secretion' led him to conditioned (temporary) reflexes, and that he worked on the formation of conditioned reflexes until his death in 1936. Facts synthesized; wording not reused.

sourceRecords.title: A meta-analytic review of experiments examining the effects of extrinsic rewards on intrinsic motivation
sourceRecords.provider: Deci, E. L., Koestner, R., & Ryan, R. M., Psychological Bulletin 125(6), 1999
sourceRecords.notes: Abstract verified through the Europe PMC API. Source of the effect sizes reported in the lesson: 128 studies; engagement-contingent, completion-contingent, and performance-contingent rewards undermined free-choice intrinsic motivation (d = -0.40, -0.36, -0.28); positive feedback enhanced free-choice behavior (d = 0.33) and self-reported interest (d = 0.31); tangible rewards tended to be more detrimental for children than for college students.

sourceRecords.title: Detrimental effects of reward: Reality or myth?
sourceRecords.provider: Eisenberger, R., & Cameron, J., American Psychologist 51(11), 1996
sourceRecords.notes: Abstract verified through the Europe PMC API. Used for the opposing position in the reward debate: that detrimental effects of reward occur under restricted, avoidable conditions and that conditioning mechanisms explain both increases and decreases in task motivation.

sourceRecords.title: Intrinsic motivation and extrinsic incentives jointly predict performance: A 40-year meta-analysis
sourceRecords.provider: Cerasoli, C. P., Nicklin, J. M., & Ford, M. T., Psychological Bulletin 140(4), 2014
sourceRecords.notes: Abstract verified through the Europe PMC API. Used for the current synthesis position: across 183 samples and 212,468 participants, intrinsic motivation was a medium-to-strong predictor of performance whether or not incentives were present; intrinsic motivation mattered less when incentives were directly tied to performance ('crowding out') and more when they were indirectly tied; incentives better predicted quantity of performance and intrinsic motivation better predicted quality; the two are described as not necessarily antagonistic.

sourceRecords.title: Evidence Review for Teacher Praise to Improve Students' Classroom Behavior (ERIC EJ1199732)
sourceRecords.provider: Moore, T. C., Maggin, D. M., Thompson, K. M., Gordon, J. R., Daniels, S., & Lang, L. E., Journal of Positive Behavior Interventions 21(1), 2019
sourceRecords.notes: Systematic review of 30 studies, 11 of which met Council for Exceptional Children and What Works Clearinghouse methodological standards; concluded there was insufficient evidence to identify teacher praise as an evidence-based practice for K-12 students without severe disabilities, with no discernible pattern for when or for whom praise works. Used for the lesson's honest-limits section.

sourceRecords.title: The Little Albert controversy: Intuition, confirmation bias, and logic
sourceRecords.notes: Abstract verified through the Europe PMC API. Supports the lesson's cautious treatment of the Watson and Rayner 'Little Albert' study as a historically disputed case rather than a settled demonstration.
